title: Going to a Better School: Effects and Behavioral Responses
research_question: Does attending a higher-achieving secondary school cause better academic outcomes for marginal students, and how do students, parents, teachers, and peers adjust their behavior in response to being placed in a stronger school environment? In particular, do gains in peer quality translate into improved exit-exam performance, and through what behavioral channels?
data_description: The study combines administrative records and original survey data from Romania. The administrative data cover the universe of Romanian towns (excluding Bucharest and single-school towns) for the 2001-2003 high school admission cohorts, linking each student's end-of-middle-school transition score to school/track placement and to subsequent Baccalaureate exam taking and grades. Survey data were collected in 2005-2007 in 71 targeted towns (with 59-64 successfully completing surveys), covering students, parents, and teachers in schools near admission cutoffs. Key variables include transition scores, school- and track-level average peer scores, Baccalaureate outcomes, teacher characteristics (certification, experience), parental behaviors (volunteering, helping with homework, paying for tutoring), child homework effort, perceived class rank, and negative peer interactions. Observations are at the student, parent, track, and school levels.
institutional_context: In Romania, students transition from middle school to high school through a centralized admission system. Each student receives a 'transition score' based on prior grades and a national test, and uses this score to apply to high schools and tracks (Math, Technical, Humanities, Social Science) within their town. Schools admit students in strict order of transition scores until capacity is filled, generating sharp admission cutoffs that vary by school and track and by cohort. Towns typically contain multiple high schools of differing selectivity, so students with scores just above a school's cutoff enter a higher-achieving peer environment than students just below. At the end of high school, students take the Baccalaureate, a standardized national exam whose grade is observable in administrative records, providing a common achievement measure across schools and tracks.
